#### Inflation FAQs

#### What is inflation?

Inflation measures the rise in the price of a representative basket of goods and services. Headline inflation is usually expressed as a percentage change on a month-on-month (MoM) and year-on-year (YoY) basis. Core inflation excludes more volatile elements such as food and fuel which can fluctuate because of geopolitical and seasonal factors. Core inflation is the figure economists focus on and is the level targeted by central banks, which are mandated to keep inflation at a manageable level, usually around 2%.

#### What is the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices of a basket of goods and services over a period of time. It is usually expressed as a percentage change on a month-on-month (MoM) and year-on-year (YoY) basis. Core CPI is the figure targeted by central banks as it excludes volatile food and fuel inputs. When Core CPI rises above 2% it usually results in higher interest rates and vice versa when it falls below 2%. Since higher interest rates are positive for a currency, higher inflation usually results in a stronger currency. The opposite is true when inflation falls.

#### What is the impact of inflation on foreign exchange?

Although it may seem counter-intuitive, high inflation in a country pushes up the value of its currency and vice versa for lower inflation. This is because the central bank will normally raise interest rates to combat the higher inflation, which attract more global capital inflows from investors looking for a lucrative place to park their money.

#### How does inflation influence the price of Gold?

Formerly, Gold was the asset investors turned to in times of high inflation because it preserved its value, and whilst investors will often still buy Gold for its safe-haven properties in times of extreme market turmoil, this is not the case most of the time. This is because when inflation is high, central banks will put up interest rates to combat it.
Higher interest rates are negative for Gold because they increase the opportunity-cost of holding Gold vis-a-vis an interest-bearing asset or placing the money in a cash deposit account. On the flipside, lower inflation tends to be positive for Gold as it brings interest rates down, making the bright metal a more viable investment alternative.

title: US Dollar Price Forecast: Dollar Steadies Before PCE, DXY Holds 103.80 as EUR/USD, GBP/USD Stall Below Pivots
content_md:
#### **Dollar Pauses Ahead of Final Inflation Test Before Fed Meeting**

The dollar steadied on Wednesday after a 0.44% slide on Tuesday, as traders waited for US inflation and growth data, the last major readings before the Fed's December policy meeting, Reuters reported. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, was flat at 103.85.

#### **Dollar: All Eyes on PCE and GDP**

Traders see a 97% chance of a Fed hike in December and a 66% chance of another increase in January, according to CME FedWatch, which turns futures prices into rate odds, Reuters said. "The whole of November has been a really, really strong month for the US dollar," said Rodrigo Catril, senior FX strategist at National Australia Bank.

The BEA releases its October personal income and outlays report and the second estimate of third-quarter GDP at 8:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, is expected to show a 0.3% rise in October after a 0.5% gain the month before, while GDP growth is expected at an annualised 3.5%, Reuters said. US consumer confidence also rose more than expected in November to its highest in nearly two years. In my view, a softer PCE reading is the main risk to the dollar this week, since a hike is already almost fully priced.

#### **Euro: ECB Hike Talk Offers Little Help**

The euro was little changed at $1.0961, Reuters said. The dollar hit a more than 19-month high against the euro on Monday, according to Reuters. ECB policymaker Olaf Sleijpen said on Tuesday that the central bank is likely to raise rates in December.

Economists already expect that move: all 71 economists in a Reuters poll taken November 10-12 forecast a hike in the deposit rate to 2.75% in December.

#### **Sterling: BoE Bets Cooled**

Sterling was little changed at $1.3106, Reuters said. Investors trimmed bets on a December Bank of England hike after UK inflation came in below the central bank's forecast on November 18, and money markets priced about a 79% chance of a hike last Friday, Reuters reported. The BoE's next policy decision is on December 17.

#### **US Dollar Index Technical Analysis: DXY Holds 103.80 Pivot and Rising Trendline**

On the 4-hour chart, the US Dollar Index is trading near 103.99. After a pullback from near 104.54, buyers stepped in at 103.80, the pivot point, a level calculated from the previous period's high, low and close that traders use to judge direction. That level lines up with a rising trendline, a line connecting higher lows since November 10, and both moving averages, which track average prices over time, are rising below price.

#### Quick Read

- JPIE and BINC both paid roughly 6% over the past year, but those trailing payouts are not yields to maturity or promises of future income.
- JPIE returned just 3% over a year against a 6% payout rate, and BINC returned around 1%, so share price losses ate into each check.
- Neither fund has a maturity date, so retirees needing principal back on a known date get that certainty only from the Treasury.

The 10-year Treasury yielded 4.92% on Monday, November 23, according to the U.S. Treasury's daily par yield curve. A 10-year Treasury note appeals to retirees for three reasons: it pays fixed interest every six months, returns its face value on a specified maturity date, and is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. That said, over the past year, two actively managed bond ETFs paid out more than the 10-year Treasury yields now. Based on delayed premarket quotes from the morning of Tuesday, November 24, **JPMorgan Income ETF** (NYSEARCA:JPIE) paid 5.7% of its $45.01 share price over the trailing twelve months. **iShares Flexible Income Active ETF** (NYSEARCA:BINC) paid 6.06% of its $50.53 share price. JPIE shares a sponsor with JPMorgan's popular equity premium income fund, but it runs a separate strategy built entirely around bonds. Before you trade a Treasury for either fund, look at what those payouts actually measure.
